pos: n. (proper name; a man of Judah, and the father of David's overseer of tillage)
etymology: Hebrew Kelub, of uncertain meaning; a connection with a word for a basket or cage has been proposed. The name is distinct from Chelubai, the alternate name of Caleb son of Hezron.
biblical_def: Chelub is the name of two men, both of Judah. The first stands in the genealogy: “And Chelub the brother of Shuah begat Mehir, which was the father of Eshton” (1 Chronicles 4:11). The second is named as a father in David's civil register: “And over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub” (1 Chronicles 27:26). The dictionary keeps the name distinct from Chelubai, which 1 Chronicles 2:9 gives as another name for Caleb son of Hezron; the forms are near but the men are not the same. What is worth noting is the neighbourhood this name keeps. Two verses before the first Chelub stands one of the best-known prayers in Scripture, offered by a man with a name that meant sorrow: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10). The driest genealogy in the Bible has a prayer buried in it, answered.

corruption_summary: Genealogies are read as inert lists; Judah's holds an answered prayer and the names of men who served a king.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapters of 1 Chronicles 1 to 9 are the most skipped pages in the Bible, dismissed as a wall of names. They are not inert. Two verses from Chelub stands Jabez's prayer and the plain statement that God granted it; a few verses further the Chronicler notes a potter's town, a scribe's family, a man with no sons and an Egyptian servant who married his daughter. The lists are full of households with histories.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's record keeps what men would not. A man is in Scripture because he had a brother and a grandson; another because his son managed ploughland for David. The dictionary treats these names as worth an entry for the same reason the Holy Ghost thought them worth a verse.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the sons of Pahath-moab in Ezra's register)
etymology: Hebrew Kelal, commonly read completeness or perfection, from a root meaning to complete or to make perfect — the root behind kalil, a whole burnt offering.
biblical_def: Chelal is named once: “And of the sons of Pahathmoab; Adna, and Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezaleel, and Binnui, and Manasseh” (Ezra 10:30). He stands in the register of Ezra 10, among those who had married wives of the peoples of the land and separated from them. Eight men of one house are named in his verse — the sons of Pahath-moab, a family that had returned from Babylon in large numbers under Zerubbabel and that appears again among the builders of Nehemiah's wall. His name means completeness, and the dictionary notes the irony without pressing it: a man named perfection appears in Scripture in a list of men who had sinned and were putting it right. That is in fact where completeness is found in this book. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The register closes with a flat sentence that forbids any softening: “All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children” (Ezra 10:44). No one is excused and no one is hidden.

corruption_summary: A published list of sinners is read as shaming; in Scripture the naming is the confession and the mercy follows it.
corruption_paragraphs: To modern instinct a register of named offenders looks like public humiliation, and the chapter is read as cruelty. The men themselves had proposed the covenant and answered Ezra with one voice; the list is their confession in writing, not an exposure imposed on them. Scripture's way with sin is to name it, and its way with a confessed sinner is to show mercy.

The principle to recover is the order of Proverbs 28:13: covering sin forfeits prosperity, confessing and forsaking obtains mercy. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9). A man named completeness is found in a list of the repentant, which is the only place in Scripture completeness is ever found.

pos: n. (proper name; one named in Ezra's register of those who separated)
etymology: Hebrew Keluhu, of uncertain meaning; the form is read by some as connected with completion, as with Chelal, and by others as a variant of a name meaning he hath completed.
biblical_def: Chelluh is named once, and his verse is three words: “Benaiah, Bedeiah, Chelluh” (Ezra 10:35). He stands among the sons of Bani in the register of Ezra 10, one of the longest lists of named individuals in the Old Testament — well over a hundred men, enumerated house by house, each of whom had married a wife of the peoples of the land and put her away. The dictionary records the difficulty of the chapter honestly and does not resolve it by pretending the cost was small. What the chapter claims for itself is that the law was read, the people assembled in the rain, the men themselves proposed the remedy, and the matter was carried out by a commission over three months with the names written down. Chelluh is one of those names. There is no sentence of Scripture that tells us what became of him afterward. The record keeps the accounting and leaves the rest with God, which is what a register does: it establishes who was present and what was done, and trusts the Judge of all the earth to do right.

corruption_summary: Hard passages are either defended with bravado or quietly dropped; Scripture asks neither, and leaves the Judge to be just.
corruption_paragraphs: There are two common ways of mishandling Ezra 10. One is to celebrate it as though the cost were nothing; the other is to set it aside as unworthy of the God of the New Testament. The dictionary takes neither course. The chapter records men trembling in the rain, a commission sitting three months, and a list of names, and it offers no commentary on how any of those households fared.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture may be trusted where it is not fully explained. “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25) is Abraham's question and the Bible's answer, and a reader who holds it can face a chapter like this one without either bluster or embarrassment.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Azel in the Benjamite line of Saul)
etymology: Hebrew Bokeru, commonly read his firstborn or youth, from bekor (firstborn). Some read the word in these verses as a description rather than a name.
biblical_def: Bocheru is named twice, in two nearly identical verses: “And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel” (1 Chronicles 8:38), repeated at 1 Chronicles 9:44. He belongs to the Benjamite genealogy that the Chronicler gives twice over, and the reason for the repetition is the line it traces: Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul, and Saul begat Jonathan — this is the house of Israel's first king, carried down through many generations past the end of the dynasty. That is a striking piece of record-keeping. Saul's reign ended in disaster on Gilboa, and the Chronicler states the reason without softening: “So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD” (1 Chronicles 10:13). Yet the family is enrolled, twice, down to Azel's six sons. God did not blot out the house He had set aside from the throne. The dictionary marks the mercy in that: rejection from an office is not rejection from the people, and a king's failure did not erase his great-grandchildren from the book.

corruption_summary: A rejected house is assumed erased; the Chronicler enrols Saul's descendants twice while naming Saul's sin plainly.
corruption_paragraphs: Where a dynasty falls, the expectation is that the record will bury it, and the critical assumption is that Chronicles exists to glorify David at Saul's expense. The book does both of the things that assumption cannot hold together: it states Saul's transgression and the reason for his death in the bluntest terms, and it preserves his family tree through many generations, giving it twice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between losing an office and losing a place among God's people. Saul was rejected from the kingship; Jonathan died a faithful friend; Mephibosheth ate at David's table; and Azel's six sons are written in the book. God's judgments are exact, and they are not indiscriminate.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Bunah, understanding or discretion, from the root bin, to discern — the same root as binah, the understanding that Proverbs commands a man to get.
biblical_def: Bunah is named once: “And the sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were, Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah” (1 Chronicles 2:25). He is second of five sons in the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah — a line that runs parallel to the line of Ram through which David came, and that the Chronicler traces at length for its own sake. His name is one of the great words of the wisdom books: binah, understanding. “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding” (Proverbs 4:7). The dictionary notes the sort of understanding Scripture means by it, because the word has been emptied in modern use. Biblical understanding is not neutral analytic capacity; it begins in a particular place and nowhere else: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding” (Proverbs 9:10). A man may be clever without it and may not be wise without it. Bunah is a name and nothing more in the record, but the name is a word his parents meant.

corruption_summary: Understanding is treated as neutral intellectual capacity; Scripture roots it in the fear of the LORD and the knowledge of the holy.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern academy treats understanding as a method available to anyone who reasons carefully, with God as one possible object of study among others. Proverbs locates it differently and without hedging: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the holy is understanding. On that account a man may hold a great deal of information and have no understanding at all.

The principle to recover is that knowledge has a starting point which is not itself neutral. “Lean not unto thine own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5) is not anti-intellectual; it is the ordering of the intellect under revelation. A son of Judah named understanding carried in his name a word that the Bible refuses to let float free of its author.

pos: n. (proper name; a man in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Qots, a thorn — the ordinary word for a thorn or brier, the same word used of the thorns that choke the seed and of the briers of the wilderness.
biblical_def: Coz is named once: “And Coz begat Anub, and Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum” (1 Chronicles 4:8). He stands in the Judah genealogy a few verses after Jabez, and his name is thorn. The dictionary pauses on that, because the thorn is one of Scripture's great images and it carries the whole history of the fall and the redemption. Thorns came with the curse: “cursed is the ground for thy sake … thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:17-18). Thorns are what choke the word in the parable. Paul's affliction was a thorn in the flesh, and he was told that God's strength was made perfect in his weakness. And at the end a crown of thorns was plaited and pressed on the head of Christ, so that the sign of the curse was worn by the One who was made a curse for us: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). A man named Thorn is a line in a genealogy; the word in his name runs from Eden to Calvary.

corruption_summary: The curse on the ground is treated as myth; Scripture traces thorns from Eden to the crown pressed on Christ's head.
corruption_paragraphs: A historical fall and a real curse on the creation are widely abandoned, with Genesis 3 read as a story about the human condition rather than an event. The dictionary holds a historical Adam and a real curse, and notes that the whole Bible is built on it: if the ground was not cursed, the thorn means nothing, and if the thorn means nothing, the crown of thorns is only cruelty and not a sign.

The principle to recover is that Christ took the curse itself upon Himself. “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The soldiers who plaited that crown were mocking a king; they were in fact crowning Him with the emblem of the judgment He had come to bear. A man named Thorn sits in the line that led to Him.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Naarai, one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ezbai, of uncertain meaning; a connection with a word for the hyssop plant or with a root for shining has been proposed, neither with certainty.
biblical_def: Ezbai is named once, and only as a father: “Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai” (1 Chronicles 11:37). His son stands in the roll of David's mighty men; the parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:35 gives the corresponding place to “Paarai the Arbite,” one of the several points at which the two musters differ in a name. The dictionary records that without alarm, as it does the other variants: the Masoretic tradition preserves what it received, and no doctrine turns on it. What is worth marking is how these rolls end. 2 Samuel 23 closes its list with a single name that darkens everything above it — “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). The last of David's mighty men is the man David had killed to cover an adultery. Scripture puts him there and says nothing further. The register of the king's bravest men ends with the name of his worst sin, and the book that records both is the same book that records his repentance in the fifty-first Psalm.

corruption_paragraphs: The charge that the Bible was composed to burnish its kings runs into 2 Samuel 23:39. A document written to flatter David does not end the catalogue of his finest soldiers with Uriah the Hittite, and it does not include Psalm 51. The record keeps the sin next to the glory and lets the reader feel the weight of the juxtaposition.

The principle to recover is the honesty of inspired Scripture about its own subjects, and the completeness of repentance where God grants it. “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4) is in the Bible because David wrote it and God kept it. A faith whose records conceal nothing has nothing to fear from examination.

pos: n. (proper name; a descendant of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ephlal, commonly read judge or he hath judged, from the root palal, to intervene or to judge — the root that also gives the common word for prayer, tephillah.
biblical_def: Ephlal is named once, and in a verse that names him twice: “And Zabad begat Ephlal, and Ephlal begat Obed” (1 Chronicles 2:37). He stands in a remarkable stretch of the Jerahmeelite line. A few verses earlier the Chronicler records that “Sheshan had no sons, but daughters,” and that he gave his daughter to Jarha his Egyptian servant to wife, and she bore him Attai (1 Chronicles 2:34-35) — and the line that runs down through Ephlal to Obed and on to Azariah and Jehu descends from that marriage. An Egyptian bondman married into Judah, and his descendants are enrolled in the tribe of the promise for fourteen generations. The dictionary notes this alongside Bithiah the Pharaoh's daughter: Judah's genealogy holds an Egyptian servant and an Egyptian princess, both brought in. The root of Ephlal's name gives both to judge and to pray, which is fitting in a line that existed because a man with no sons made a decision about his daughter and God honoured the house that came of it.

corruption_summary: Israel's tribes are imagined as closed bloodlines; Judah's own genealogy descends in part from an Egyptian servant.
corruption_paragraphs: The picture of Old Testament Israel as a sealed ethnic community is hard to hold against 1 Chronicles 2. Sheshan had no sons; he gave his daughter to Jarha, an Egyptian slave; and the Chronicler then traces their descendants through fourteen named generations as a branch of Judah. Ephlal is in that branch, and so the tribe of the sceptre carries an Egyptian servant's blood in its record.

The principle to recover is that God is no respecter of persons, which Peter learned at Caesarea and which the genealogies had been quietly saying all along. “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). An Egyptian bondman and a Pharaoh's daughter both appear in Judah's line, and the Chronicler names them without apology.

pos: n. (proper name; a descendant of Saul in the Benjamite genealogy)
etymology: Hebrew Bin'a, of uncertain meaning; a connection with ben (son) or with a root for fountains has been proposed, neither with certainty.
biblical_def: Binea is named twice, in the two passes the Chronicler makes over Saul's line: “And Moza begat Binea: Rapha was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son” (1 Chronicles 8:37), and “And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son” (1 Chronicles 9:43). The two verses differ by one name — Rapha in the first, Rephaiah in the second — which the dictionary records as the ordinary kind of variation between two passes over a long list, touching nothing doctrinal. Binea stands five generations below Jonathan, in a family that had every reason to disappear from the record. The line descends from Jonathan through Merib-baal, who is Mephibosheth, the lame son David sought out for Jonathan's sake and set at the king's table continually. “So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem: for he did eat continually at the king's table” (2 Samuel 9:13). That kindness was shown for the sake of a covenant David had made with a dead friend. Binea is one of the names that exist downstream of a promise kept to a man who could not enforce it.

corruption_summary: A fallen dynasty's survivors are expected to be erased; David sought them out to keep a covenant with a dead friend.
corruption_paragraphs: Ancient politics would have required the new house to extinguish the old, and critics of Chronicles assume that the record serves David against Saul. The narrative does the opposite at the decisive point. David asks whether any of Saul's house is left that he may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake, finds a lame grandson, restores his lands, and seats him at the royal table for life.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is covenant faithfulness toward those who cannot repay or compel it. Jonathan was dead and Mephibosheth was helpless, and the kindness was shown anyway, because a covenant had been made. It is the clearest Old Testament picture of grace to the undeserving, and Binea's name is in the Bible because that line was spared.

etymology: Hebrew Bariach, commonly read fugitive or fleeing, from a root meaning to flee or to pass through swiftly.
biblical_def: Bariah is named once: “And the sons of Shechaniah; Shemaiah: and the sons of Shemaiah; Hattush, and Igeal, and Bariah, and Neariah, and Shaphat, six” (1 Chronicles 3:22). The chapter is the royal genealogy of David, and its last section carries the line past the captivity — through Jeconiah, through Zerubbabel who led the return, and down several further generations to names like this one. That is the most quietly important fact in the chapter. Nebuchadnezzar had burned the temple, broken the walls, blinded Zedekiah and killed his sons, and the house of David was reduced to a prisoner eating at a foreign king's table. And the line continued, and the Chronicler could still write it down. “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10) held through the fire. Matthew and Luke both pick up this line and carry it to Joseph and Mary. A man named fugitive stands in the pedigree of the house that had fled, been taken, and not been ended, because a promise stood over it that Babylon could not reach.

corruption_summary: The exile is read as the end of the Davidic promise; Chronicles traces the line straight through it and out the other side.
corruption_paragraphs: A common reading treats the fall of Jerusalem as the collapse of the Davidic hope, with the later messianic expectation a reinterpretation after the fact. 1 Chronicles 3 is the answer written as a list. The chapter runs the royal line through Jeconiah the captive, through Zerubbabel the governor, and on to men like Bariah, generations after the throne had ceased to exist.

The principle to recover is that God's promises survive the worst that history can do to them. “David shall never want a man to sit upon the throne of the house of Israel” (Jeremiah 33:17) was said as Jerusalem was falling, and it was kept, though not in the way anyone watching the walls come down could have traced. The genealogy that names a man called fugitive ends in the Gospels, at a manger.
